conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You're here because of worsening abdominal pain near your G-tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been getting worse since my last discharge. It’s deep around the tube and in my upper belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea, vomiting, or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just some nausea. No vomiting, no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I see you had a G-tube exchange in clinic yesterday and the pain got worse after that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It spiked right after. I thought it might settle, but it hasn’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your labs and get a CT scan to make sure there’s no infection or other issue around the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected? The skin looks a little red.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s some redness and a little drainage, but no spreading warmth or pus. Bariatric surgery saw you and thinks it might be superficial, but we’ll confirm with imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain—could it be my ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible. You have a history of marginal ulcers, and that can cause deep epigastric pain. We’ll keep managing it while we investigate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back—white blood cell count is normal, no sign of infection. Kidneys, liver, and glucose are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And your chest X-ray shows no free air, so no sign of a perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. The G-tube is in the right place, balloon inflated in the stomach. There are some inflammatory changes in the muscle around the tube site, but no abscess or bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No deep infection. The inflammation might be from the recent tube manipulation. But since you’re not running a fever and your labs are clean, we don’t think you need antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why does it still hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be a combination—your known marginal ulcer, irritation from the tube changes, and possibly even the pain medicine itself. Sometimes long-term opioids can make pain more sensitive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know that could happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s called opioid-induced hyperalgesia. We’ll keep you on oxycodone for now but watch that closely. We also restarted your tube feeds to keep your blood sugar stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing that at home, but I keep forgetting to check my sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking it every six hours here. It’s been stable. You must keep the feeds running continuously to avoid hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, maybe 6 out of 10 now. Still constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your blood pressure was low this morning—88 over 74. You were asymptomatic, but we think it’s from the atenolol and maybe some dehydration from the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My BP is always low when I’m in pain. I usually stop the atenolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you fluids and stopped the atenolol. We recommend not restarting it. Beta blockers can mask low blood sugar symptoms, which is risky for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Better to manage your heart rate without hiding hypoglycemia signs. We’ll discuss alternatives with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show your white count dropped a bit—3.8—but it’s not concerning since you’re not sick. Hemoglobin is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the pain or the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be stress-related. We’ll monitor it. The important thing is you’re not bleeding or infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is improving, vitals stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with oxycodone 10 mg every 4 hours as needed—84 tablets for two weeks. Plus Tylenol for baseline. But you’ll need to follow up with pain management for refills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liquid oxycodone? I couldn’t find it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Crushing pills in the tube isn’t safe. We’ll help you locate the liquid form. It’s easier on your system and avoids tube clogs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, keep using the mupirocin on the tube site twice daily to prevent infection. And continue your Prevacid and Carafate for the ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the EGD? Wasn’t I supposed to have that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, still planned. Follow up with GI—they’ll schedule it. It’ll help us check the ulcer directly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my atenolol—I won’t restart it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we advise against it. Talk to your doctor about other options. Safety first with your hypoglycemia risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Follow up with your PCP in a week, and bariatric surgery if pain worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check—pain is at 5, you’re moving well, and your vitals are stable. All set for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Thanks for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if pain gets worse or you run into issues with meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.
